conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re transferring you to Vascular Surgery today. They’ll manage your upcoming toe amputation. You were scheduled for a TMA, but we’ll see what’s best.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Is the gangrene worse? I was hoping it might improve.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Actually, it’s looking a bit better. We may only need to remove one or two toes instead of a larger amputation. We’ll decide in the OR.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning. You’re due for dialysis today. After that, we’ll finalize plans for surgery tomorrow.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Will I be on heparin again like last time?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, we’ve started a heparin drip to keep your blood thin, especially with your mechanical valve. Your INR was low on admission.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: After dialysis, your blood pressure spiked again. We gave IV hydralazine, and it’s coming down. The chest X-ray shows fluid in your lungs—common with volume overload.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So that’s why I felt short of breath?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Exactly. Dialysis should help remove the extra fluid. We’ll keep monitoring your BP.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You had another episode of nausea and high BP this morning. We gave you a scopolamine patch and Zofran. O2 helped with the breathing.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’m ready for this over with. When’s the surgery?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re going to the OR in a few hours. You’ll have a left toe amputation—likely just the first and second toes. You’ll be under anesthesia and wake up in recovery.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Hi, you’re back. The surgery went well. You had amputation of the first and second toes on the left foot. The gangrene was limited, so we didn’t need a larger procedure.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s a relief. Is the wound okay?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: It looks clean. We’ll keep an eye on it. You’re on Dilaudid for pain—we increased the dose because your foot hurt more after dialysis.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good news—your nausea is gone, and you’re eating. BP is much better—120s over 70s—on labetalol, amlodipine, and hydralazine.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Why the new blood pressure meds?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Cardiology and Nephrology suggested switching from metoprolol to labetalol—it’s better for patients on dialysis. Hydralazine helps too.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And the warfarin? I was on that before.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We restarted Coumadin yesterday. Your INR hit 2.0, so we stopped the heparin drip. You’ll go home on warfarin—5 mg tonight.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Should I watch for bleeding?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes—watch for unusual bruising, nosebleeds, or dark stools. Your PCP will manage your INR checks.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your wound vac on the right stump was changed today—looks great with healthy tissue. Left foot wound is clean too.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’m glad it’s healing. What about driving or walking?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: No driving until cleared. You can use your heel to pivot, but keep the left foot elevated when possible. No heavy lifting over 20 pounds.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Can I shower?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, but don’t soak the foot. No baths or pools for four weeks. Sutures come out in about three weeks at your vascular clinic visit.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re doing really well. We’re clearing you for discharge today. You’ll have home health for wound care and PT.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s great. What about my blood pressure meds long-term?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Cardiology suggested lisinopril instead of hydralazine, but we’ll let your nephrologist decide. You have an appointment with Dr. ___ this week?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes, I do. And I’ll see the vascular surgeon for stitches?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, in about three weeks. Call if you see redness, drainage, fever, or new pain in the foot.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And the pain meds? They make me constipated.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Take them as needed. Increase fiber and fluids. We’ve included stool softeners in your instructions.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ll try. Thank you for everything.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re welcome. We’ve set up a cardiology appointment too. Take care, and follow up closely.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I will. I’m just glad to be going home.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ll get your discharge papers ready. The home health team will be there this afternoon.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And I take warfarin tonight, right?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, 5 mg tonight. Then follow up with your PCP for INR checks.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Got it. Thank you again.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re doing great. Just keep up with your appointments and call if anything changes.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I will. I’m feeling much better already.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s what we like to hear. We’ll see you in clinic soon.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Looking forward to it. Thanks for explaining everything.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Of course. Take care, Ms. ___.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: You too.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Nurse will be in with your discharge meds and instructions.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay, I’m ready.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Great. We’ll get you out of here soon.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Appreciate it.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Take it easy at home and keep that foot elevated.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I will. Thank you.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re welcome. Have a safe trip home.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good evening, Ms. ___? I'm Dr. ___ from the internal medicine team. I understand you came in with some confusion and low oxygen. Can you tell me how you're feeling now?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’m feeling better now, thank you. I was really out of it earlier. My husband said I wasn’t making sense when I woke up. And I couldn’t catch my breath.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, your oxygen level dropped into the mid-80s today. That’s quite low. You’re on oxygen now and your levels have improved to the 90s. We think the low oxygen was due to fluid buildup in your lungs.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Oh, okay. I’ve been on dialysis for years, so I know I have to watch my fluids. I did feel more short of breath lying down.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Exactly. Your chest X-ray shows some fluid in your lungs and a known pleural effusion on the right may have gotten a bit worse. We’ll get you scheduled for dialysis tomorrow to remove the extra fluid.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That makes sense. I had dialysis two days ago, but maybe it wasn’t enough.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Possibly. We’ll work with your dialysis team to make sure you’re getting the right amount removed. Now, about the confusion—did you notice anything strange before coming in?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ve been nauseous for a few days and only eating small amounts. And I’ve been more tired. My husband said I seemed confused a few times when I woke up.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We checked your labs. Your potassium was high at first, but that was likely due to a damaged blood sample. The repeat was normal. Your kidney function is stable for your baseline. But we’re concerned about your medications possibly contributing to the confusion.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Medications? I take a lot, I know. Pain pills, nerve medicine, sleep aids…

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, you're on several medications that affect the brain—like OxyContin, Dilaudid, gabapentin, lorazepam, and zolpidem. In someone on dialysis, these can build up and cause drowsiness or confusion, especially when combined.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Oh. I didn’t realize they could do that together.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: It’s very common. We’ve already stopped lorazepam, gabapentin, and ropinirole. We’ll also lower your OxyContin dose to see if that helps your mental clarity.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ve wanted to cut back on the pain meds. My leg pain is better since the toe surgery, but I still get breakthrough pain.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ll keep Dilaudid available for breakthrough pain, but we’ll space it out to every six hours instead of every three. And we’ll use Tylenol as support—you can take up to 4 grams a day.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay, that sounds good. I don’t want to be foggy all the time.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning. Your dialysis was completed about an hour ago. They removed about 3 liters of fluid. How are you feeling?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I feel lighter. And I can breathe much better. I’m not using the oxygen as much.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s great. Your oxygen saturation is 97% on room air. The crackles in your lungs have improved. This confirms the fluid was the main issue.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So the confusion was from the meds and the low oxygen?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Most likely, yes. The CT scan of your head showed no stroke or bleeding. Your mental status is much clearer now, which supports that idea.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’m glad it wasn’t something more serious.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We reviewed your labs. Your liver enzyme AST was mildly elevated, but it’s likely from the recent surgery. Your LDH was high when you arrived but has now normalized.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Is that a sign of infection or heart problem?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We considered that, but your troponin is normal and blood cultures show no infection. The LDH was likely from tissue stress after surgery and has resolved.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay, good to know.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your second dialysis session is scheduled for tomorrow. Another 3 liters will be removed. Your blood pressure is stable—150 over 60 this morning.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ve been on labetalol, amlodipine, and hydralazine since my last hospital stay. Are we keeping those?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, and we’re increasing your labetalol from 200 mg three times a day to 400 mg three times a day to help with blood pressure and heart protection.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay. And my warfarin? I’m on it for my mechanical valve.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your INR was 2.3, which is in the safe range. You’ll continue warfarin daily. No need for heparin bridge this time.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Good. I don’t like the shots.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: The vascular surgery team checked your left foot. The amputation site is healing well. No signs of infection or new gangrene.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ve been keeping it clean and elevated like they said.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Excellent. You’ll continue with home wound care. A nurse will visit to check the dressing.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’ve completed both dialysis sessions and are now euvolemic—no extra fluid. Your oxygen is 98% on room air. We’re planning for discharge tomorrow.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s great news. What about my pain meds?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re on 20 mg of OxyContin twice daily now, down from 30 mg. We’re giving you a weaning plan: 20 mg for two weeks, then 15, then 10, then 5 mg.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And the Dilaudid?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You can use it every six hours as needed. Try to use Tylenol first. Don’t stop cold turkey—tapering avoids withdrawal.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Got it. And I’m not taking gabapentin or lorazepam anymore?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Correct. We stopped both. If restless legs return, talk to your primary doctor about restarting ropinirole.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Doctor, will I need oxygen at home?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: No, you’re breathing well on room air. You can discontinue home oxygen unless symptoms return.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: One more thing—we restarted sodium thiosulfate, 12.5 mg on dialysis days. It helps with dialysis-related issues and was part of your prior regimen.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes, I remember that. It’s good to have it back.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re cleared for discharge. Your mental status is clear, you’re breathing well, and your fluid status is stable.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thank you. I feel much better than when I came in.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ll send the prescriptions to your pharmacy. Follow up with your nephrologist, vascular surgeon, and primary doctor within the next two weeks.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I will. Thanks for helping me sort through all my meds.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re very welcome. Take care, and call if you have trouble with breathing, confusion, or wound issues.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I will. Have a good day.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Just a quick check-in before you leave. Any last questions?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Hello, I'm Dr. Lee. I’ll be helping take care of you during your stay. Can you tell me what brought you to the hospital?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Hi, Doctor. I’ve had dark, tarry stools for the past two days. I’m not in pain, but I’ve been feeling weak and tired.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I see. That can be a sign of bleeding in the digestive tract. We checked your blood and your hemoglobin was low at 8.0, so we gave you one unit of blood in the ER and will likely give more.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Oh, that makes sense. I’ve been dizzy too. Is it serious?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: It’s concerning, especially with your medical history. You’re on warfarin for your mechanical heart valve, so we have to be careful. We’ve stopped the warfarin for now and started an IV heparin drip to keep your blood thin but reduce bleeding risk.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay, that sounds scary. Will I need surgery?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Not right now. We’re going to do an upper endoscopy today to look in your stomach and upper intestine. A colonoscopy is scheduled for tomorrow to check your colon.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Alright. And my dialysis? I do it five times a week at home.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ve coordinated with renal. You’ll get dialysis here while you’re in the hospital. They’ll help manage your fluids and electrolytes.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Good. My blood pressure’s been all over the place lately.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, we saw your BP was high earlier—190 over 63. We gave you labetalol. Since your home meds were stopped due to low pressures during dialysis, we’re restarting them carefully.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ve had so many changes. It’s hard to keep track.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ll go over everything before you leave. For now, focus on resting. The GI team will be in soon for your endoscopy.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning. How are you feeling?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: A little better. The scope yesterday didn’t find anything, right?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s correct. The EGD showed some mild irritation in your duodenum—duodenitis—but no active bleeding. The colonoscopy is scheduled for today.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: What’s duodenitis? Is that why I’m bleeding?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: It’s inflammation in the first part of your small intestine. It can cause bleeding, but we didn’t see any active source. We’ll check your colon today and may do a capsule study if needed.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay. And my blood? Did it improve?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your hemoglobin went up to 8.5 after the second unit of blood. We’re giving a third unit today to stabilize it further.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thank you. I feel less shaky already.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: The colonoscopy was completed. It showed angioectasia in your cecum—small abnormal blood vessels—and some polyps in the rectum.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Did they stop the bleeding?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: There was no active bleeding. The polyps were small and not bleeding. The angioectasia could be the source, but it’s not bleeding now. We’ll do a capsule study to look at your small intestine.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: How does that work?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’ll swallow a small pill-sized camera that takes pictures as it moves through your gut. It’ll help us see if there’s any bleeding higher up.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Alright. And my warfarin? When can I restart it?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re keeping the heparin drip going for now. Once we’re sure the bleeding has stopped, we’ll restart warfarin. Your mechanical valve means we can’t stop blood thinners for long.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good news—the capsule study didn’t show any active bleeding. It’s likely the bleed stopped on its own.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s a relief. Can I go home soon?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Not quite yet. We need to restart your warfarin and make sure your INR starts to rise. It’s still low at 1.8. We want it between 2.5 and 3.5 for your valve.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I remember. I had a stroke before, so I can’t afford a clot.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Exactly. We’ve started warfarin again and will keep the heparin until your INR is in range.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We placed a temporary dialysis catheter in your neck today because your usual access isn’t working. It’ll make dialysis easier while you’re here.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Is it safe? I’ve had infections before.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We used ultrasound and sterile technique. The risk is low, and we’ll remove it once you’re back on home dialysis.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your INR is now 2.0—still a bit low, but moving in the right direction. We’ll keep monitoring it.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’m feeling stronger. Can I walk a bit?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, with your walker. Just take it slow. Your leg wounds are healing, but the ulcer on your right heel needs care.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your hemoglobin is stable at 8.5. No more blood needed. We’re down to one unit of heparin and warfarin is working.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Great. What about my blood pressure meds?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ve increased your labetalol to 300 mg three times a day. It’s helping. Keep taking it until your nephrologist adjusts it with home dialysis.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your INR is 2.2 today—still below goal, but you’re improving. We’ve stopped the heparin.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Can I go home? I promise to follow up.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’d prefer to keep you until your INR is in range, but we understand. If you go home, you must check your INR at your next dialysis and call the results in.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I will. I’ll take the 7 mg warfarin dose you prescribed.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good. Also, keep taking pantoprazole for stomach protection, and restart aspirin as listed.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re cleared for discharge tomorrow. Your dialysis is scheduled for the day after, then home sessions resume.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thank you. What should I watch for at home?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Call if you see black stools again, feel dizzy, or your weight goes up more than 3 pounds in a day. That could mean fluid overload.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I weigh myself every morning. I’ll keep doing that.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Perfect. You also have follow-up with vascular surgery for your prosthetic and with GI in a few weeks.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And my kidney doctor?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, touch base with them at your next dialysis. They’ll help adjust your blood pressure meds.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning. We’re finalizing your discharge. Your INR is still 2.2, but you’re stable.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’m ready to go home. I’ll follow all the instructions.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re doing well. Take the warfarin as directed, check your INR, and call your PCP to set up a follow-up.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ll do that. Thank you for taking care of me.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re welcome. We’ll see you in follow-up. Get some rest and take care.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I will. Thank you again.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Just a quick check before you leave. Any questions?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: No, I think I’ve got it all. Medications, INR check, dialysis, and follow-ups.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Perfect. You’re doing great. Take care and we’ll see you soon.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thank you, Doctor.

conversation_lines.text: The discharge team is ready to take you home. Your husband is here, right?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes, he’s in the waiting area. I’m so glad to be going home.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’ve worked hard. Keep up the good care. Call us if anything changes.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I will. Thank you for everything.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Take care. See you soon.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Bye, Doctor.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Just calling to confirm you got home safely.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes, we’re home. I’m resting now.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good. Remember to take your warfarin tomorrow and get the INR checked at dialysis.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I won’t forget. Thank you for checking in.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re welcome. Take care.

conversation_lines.text: Final call. Your discharge summary has been sent to your PCP and nephrologist.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thank you. I’ll make sure they get it.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re all set. Rest well and we’ll see you in follow-up.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I will. Thank you again.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Take care.

conversation_lines.text: Bye.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Great. Call anytime if you need us.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I will. Thank you, Doctor.

conversation_lines.text: Hello, I'm Dr. Lee. I understand you came in because of dark, tarry stools?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes, doctor. They were black and mixed with some red blood. I’ve been feeling weak since my last hospital stay.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I see. Any pain in your belly or nausea?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: No real pain, but I did feel nauseous. And I’ve noticed I bruise easily lately.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That makes sense. Your blood work shows your hemoglobin is low at 7.9, and your INR is high—4.3. That means your blood is too thin.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Is that why I’m bleeding?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: It’s likely a big part of it. You’re on warfarin for your mechanical heart valve, but when the level gets too high, it can cause bleeding. We’ve stopped the warfarin for now.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: But won’t stopping it put me at risk for a clot?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good question. Yes, it does. But we’re starting a heparin drip to protect your heart valve while we manage the bleeding.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay, that sounds safe.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We also placed a temporary line in your groin because your dialysis access is hard to use. You’ll need dialysis tomorrow.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes, I do dialysis five times a week at home. Is my potassium okay? It’s been high before.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: It was high at 7.7, but dialysis will help bring it down. We’re watching it closely.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thank you.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We did an EGD earlier—camera down your throat—to look for the bleed. We saw mild duodenitis and a small hiatal hernia, but no active bleeding.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So no source was found?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And if it’s still bleeding?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ll monitor your blood counts. You’ve already received two units of blood, and we’ll give more if needed.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning. You had dialysis yesterday. How are you feeling?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: A little stronger. Any news from the capsule test?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So still no answer?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s a relief.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: The bleeding scan was negative—no active bleed seen. That’s actually good news.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So it stopped?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes. We think the high INR triggered a brief bleed, possibly from the duodenitis. Since you’re not actively bleeding now, we’ll restart warfarin at a lower dose.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: But won’t that start the bleeding again?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re starting with a lower dose—3 mg instead of 7 mg—to bring your INR into the safe range of 2.5 to 3.5. We’ll check it daily.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay, that makes sense.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your INR yesterday was 1.6. Today it’s 2.9—perfect. We’ll keep you on 3 mg.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So I’m safe now?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes. Your hemoglobin has held steady at 8.4, and you haven’t had any more dark stools.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Good. What about my calcium? It’s always low.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, your calcium is low at 7.8. It’s common with kidney disease. We’ve started calcitriol and extra calcium carbonate—Tums—to help.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ll keep taking those at home?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, exactly. They’re now part of your regular meds.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You had a fall yesterday?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes, I lost balance getting up. My left foot stump hurt.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Vascular surgery checked you and did a quick debridement to clean the area. It’s minor, but we’ll keep an eye on it.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Will I need more surgery?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Not now. Just wound care and pain meds. We’ll follow up with vascular surgery as an outpatient.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your labs are stable. We’re planning for discharge in two days if all goes well.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s great. What do I need to watch for at home?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Watch for black stools, dizziness, or shortness of breath. Weigh yourself daily—call if you gain more than 3 pounds.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And my INR?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You need to check it on the 20th. Call your doctor with the result. Keep taking the warfarin at 3 mg unless told otherwise.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: All your labs look good. No further bleeding, and your INR is stable.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So I can go home tomorrow?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes. We’ll arrange home health to help with wound care and check on you.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thank you. I was worried.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We understand. You’ve been through a lot. But you’re stable now.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning. You’re cleared to go home today.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’m ready. Any last instructions?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Continue all your meds, especially the new calcium and calcitriol. Watch for bleeding or swelling.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And follow up with my doctors?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes—GI, vascular surgery, and your primary doctor. And call with your INR result.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I will. Thank you for taking care of me.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re welcome. Take care, and we’ll see you in follow-up if needed.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I haven’t had any black stools since then. But I’ve been feeling weak.

conversation_lines.text: That makes sense. Your hemoglobin was low at 8.8 when you arrived. We’re watching it closely. We also did a chest X-ray because you were a bit short of breath.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay. And my heart? The pain felt like my old heart attacks.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your EKG didn’t show changes, but your troponin is slightly elevated. That means there might have been some stress or minor damage to your heart muscle.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So it’s not a full heart attack?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning. Your blood pressure has been very high at times, which may have triggered the chest pain. We’ve started a nitroglycerin drip to help.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I felt a little better last night, but the pain came back after they turned it off.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, that’s why we’re keeping it running. We’re also giving you medications to reduce the strain on your heart. But we can’t do a heart catheterization yet because your INR is still high from the warfarin.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I do feel less puffy. But I’m still tired.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s expected. Your heart is working better now. The chest X-ray today shows improvement in the lung congestion.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And the infection? Are the antibiotics helping?

conversation_lines.text: And that will stop the chest pain?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s the goal. Most patients feel relief right after the stent is placed.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re about to take you to the cath lab. You’ll be awake, but sedated. The team will open the blocked artery and place a stent.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay. I trust you.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: The procedure went well. We found a 90% blockage in your LAD and placed a drug-eluting stent. Blood flow is now restored.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I already feel different. The pressure is gone.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s great to hear. You’ll now be on two blood thinners — aspirin and clopidogrel — along with warfarin. This triple therapy reduces clot risk but increases bleeding risk, so we’ll monitor closely.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: How long do I stay on all three?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’ll stay on clopidogrel and warfarin long-term. Aspirin can be stopped after about a month, once your INR is stable.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your labs are improving. Hemoglobin is up to 9.7, and your potassium was high yesterday — over 7 — so we dialyzed you urgently.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I didn’t feel it, but I’m glad you caught it.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, high potassium can cause dangerous heart rhythms. We’ll keep a close eye on it with your dialysis schedule.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ve started you on a new blood pressure medication — amlodipine — to help control your highs without making you too dizzy.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ve been sensitive to those. When should I take it?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Take it in the evening, after dialysis. And skip it if your systolic pressure is below 120 or you feel lightheaded.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your repeat chest X-ray shows the lung fluid is clearing. The small pleural effusion is still there, but it’s not causing problems.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Do I need another X-ray later?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, your outpatient team will repeat it in a few weeks to make sure the effusion resolves.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your INR has been stable around 2.2. That’s perfect for your new goal. We’ll keep you on 3 mg warfarin daily.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And I’ll need to get it checked regularly?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, at first weekly, then less often. Your husband should know the signs of bleeding — like dark stools or unusual bruising.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your heel ulcer looks stable. We’re sending you home with collagenase ointment for daily wound care.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: The nurse has been changing it. Should I keep doing that?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, daily. Keep it clean and covered. Watch for redness, swelling, or drainage — those could mean infection.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’ve made great progress. No chest pain, breathing well, and your labs are stable. We’re planning to discharge you tomorrow.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’m ready to go home. What do I need to do after?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Continue all your home dialysis sessions. Take your medications as listed — especially the clopidogrel and warfarin.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And the aspirin?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Keep it for now. After one month of stable INR, you can stop it. But keep clopidogrel and warfarin.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And my follow-ups?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: See cardiology, nephrology, and your primary care. We’ve arranged home health to help with wound care and monitoring.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Final check — your weight is 59 kg, down from admission. You’re on room air, no pain, and your heart sounds good.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I feel much better than when I came in.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’ve done well. Just remember — if chest pain returns, call 911. Same for trouble breathing or signs of bleeding.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I will. Thank you for taking such good care of me.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re welcome. We’re discharging you today with instructions and prescriptions. Your husband will get a copy too.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Just a final visit before you leave. Any last questions?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: No, I think I understand everything. Take meds, watch for bleeding, follow up, and care for the wound.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Exactly. And keep your INR in that 1.8 to 2.5 range. We’ll see you in clinic soon.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ll make sure of it.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’ve been through a lot, but you’re in a much better place now. Take care.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thank you, Doctor.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: One more thing — your gemfibrozil is restarted. Take it as before, but let your doctor know if you have muscle pain.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I remember that from last time. I’ll watch for it.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good. And continue the calcium and calcitriol — your levels are normal now.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ve been taking them every day.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Perfect. You’re doing everything right.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I just want to stay out of the hospital.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: And you will, as long as you keep up with your care. We’re here if you need us.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I appreciate that.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: The transport team will take you home shortly. Rest well.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I will. Thank you again.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re very welcome.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ll call if anything comes up.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Please do. That’s what we’re here for.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I feel safe knowing that.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We want you to feel that way. Take care of yourself.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I will.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Have a safe trip home.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thank you.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Goodbye for now.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Hello, Mrs. ___? I'm Dr. ___, one of the hospitalists. I just want to introduce myself and make sure you're comfortable. The team has reviewed your records from the other hospital.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Hi, yes, thank you. I’m feeling a little better since they gave me that medicine for the chest pain. But I was so scared in the car—felt like someone was sitting on my chest.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I completely understand. That kind of pain is very alarming. Your troponin was slightly elevated, and your EKG showed some changes, which suggests your heart wasn’t getting enough oxygen. Given your history, we’re calling this a Type II NSTEMI—basically, a small heart injury due to imbalance between supply and demand.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ve had chest pain before, but this was different. And I didn’t take my warfarin today because I forgot. Is that bad?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: It’s okay—you’re on a lot of medications. Your INR was 1.6 last check, which is a bit low for someone with a mechanical valve. We’re starting a heparin drip tonight to protect you from clots until your warfarin kicks in.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Oh, okay. I’ve been so tired lately. My hemoglobin dropped when I was on vacation. They said it was 6.5, but I didn’t feel that bad until the chest pain.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, your labs show anemia—your hemoglobin was 8.1 when you arrived. That, combined with high blood pressure, likely contributed to the heart stress. We plan to give you a blood transfusion tomorrow to help with that.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ve had transfusions before. I just worry about bleeding—I had that GI bleed not long ago.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s a valid concern. We’ve discussed it with your cardiologist and nephrologist. We’ll keep your INR goal lower than usual—between 1.8 and 2.5—to reduce bleeding risk while still protecting your valve.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That makes sense. Thank you. And my potassium was high before—should I worry?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your potassium was 5.9, which is elevated, and your EKG showed some changes. But it’s come down to 4.8 this morning, so we’re watching it closely. As long as it stays under 6, we’re okay.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning. How are you feeling today?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Morning. I feel okay—no chest pain. But I’m still tired. Did the blood help?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You received one unit yesterday, and your hemoglobin is now 9.3. We’ll check again soon. We also reviewed your recent heart cath results. Unfortunately, your anatomy isn’t suitable for another stent right now.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Oh. So what can we do?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ll focus on medical management. We’re adding two new medications: isosorbide dinitrate and ranolazine. They help reduce the heart’s workload and prevent angina.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I tried nitroglycerin before, but it made my blood pressure drop too much.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Exactly. That’s why we’re using the oral form and avoiding the spray. And for breakthrough pain, we’re prescribing dilaudid—5 mg by mouth every two hours as needed.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’d rather not come back to the hospital if I can avoid it.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re setting you up with hospice care at home. They’ll help manage your symptoms and support your goals. A palliative care doctor will come by today to talk more about your wishes.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Hi again. The palliative care team met with you and your husband. I understand you’re thinking about stopping dialysis after your son visits?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes. I’m so tired of all these treatments. I want to spend time with my family and be comfortable at home.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s completely understandable. We respect your decision. The hospice team will help you through this. For now, we’ll continue dialysis and focus on symptom control.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You just finished your dialysis session. How are you feeling?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: A bit weak, but my breathing feels better. Any news on my labs?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your hemoglobin is now 9.9, and potassium is 5.0—both much improved. Your INR is now therapeutic at 2.1, so we’re turning off the heparin drip.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s good. And my heel wound—has the nurse checked it?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, wound care consulted. They’re using Santyl and hydrogel. Keep it clean and dry. We’ll continue that at home.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Morning. We’re making good progress. Your chest pain hasn’t returned, and your breathing is stable. We’re planning to discharge you tomorrow if all goes well.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So soon? What about my medications?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re sending you home with the same meds, plus the new ones: isosorbide, ranolazine, and calcitriol for your calcium. And you’ll have dilaudid for pain, and oxygen if you’re short of breath.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And warfarin? I need to be careful with that.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, stay on 5 mg daily. We’ll monitor your INR through home health. And remember—no aspirin after one month, as discussed with your cardiologist.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Got it. And the MOLST form—I signed it. I don’t want CPR if my heart stops.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, that’s documented. Your wishes are clear and respected. Hospice will carry that forward.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Hi. Final check before discharge. Any chest pain or shortness of breath since yesterday?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: No, I feel stable. Just ready to go home.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your exam looks good. Lungs have a little crackling at the bases, but no signs of fluid overload. Weight is stable at 62 kg.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And my heart? The mechanical valve?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We hear a normal mechanical sound. No new murmurs. As long as you stay on anticoagulation, you’re protected.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And when I decide to stop dialysis, what happens?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Hospice will manage your comfort—fluids, symptoms, pain. It’s about quality of life. You’ll be supported every step of the way.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thank you. I’m scared, but also relieved to have a plan.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s completely normal. We’re here for you. The hospice nurse will visit tomorrow to set everything up.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning. Discharge is set for tomorrow. Any last questions?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Just one—will I be able to use the dilaudid if the chest pain comes back at home?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes. Take 5 mg every two hours as needed. If it doesn’t help or you feel worse, call hospice. But the goal is to keep you comfortable without coming back here.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And my son—he’s coming next week. I just want to see him.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s important. We’ll make sure everything is in place so you can focus on that time with him.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning. Today’s the day. You’re being discharged to home with hospice services.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thank you, Doctor. For everything.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re very welcome. Remember—take your meds, use oxygen as needed, and call hospice with any concerns. We’re all here to support you.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I will. I just want to be at peace.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: And you will be. Take care, Mrs. ___.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: You too.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: The transport team will be here soon to take you home.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’m ready.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ve sent all your records to hospice. They’ll call you today.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thank you again. I feel prepared.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s what we aim for. Take care, and give your son a hug for us.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I will.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Have a safe trip home.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thank you.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ll miss you, but we’re glad you’re going home.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I appreciate that.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Take it easy, and we’re always here if hospice needs us.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ll do that. Goodbye for now.
